Botmaskop Fynbos Estate and the Gated Estates of the Winelands

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We show how the wealthy and well connected in Stellenbosch are bagging valuable land for mansions for the super rich

Unique Selling Point:
We can show through both a paper trail and interviews how developers have cooked the system to get the approvals to carve up a mountainside for a luxury gated estate just outside Stellenbosch, extending the urban sprawl and angering many townsfolk.

Summary:
An half an hour walk up the mountain above Unie Park in Stellenbosch takes you to the top of the Botmaskop Fynbos Estate, which is under construction. Roads have been laid on the steep slope, and reinforced to prevent erosion, and an expensive clearvu fence erected, which I was told had been paid for by the municipality, to keep the public out. A reservoir has been erected at the top as well, which the environmentalists claim was done so illegally. On their website the developers claim that this is the highest residential estate ever approved above sea level – almost 400 metres.

But the question is this: Was it ever properly approved? Or has the rezoning of this development, and a subsequent landswap with the municipality to change its boundaries, been a sleight of hand?

There are no boards on the gate which indicate which, if any Environmental Company has done the assessment in anticipation of approval.

The property was bought and zoned in 2006 for a small mountain retreat which would be 15 chalets not exceeding 400m² each, so 6000m² of development as well as a hotel with 10 rooms not exceeding 2800m² . The rest of the 30 hectare property was zoned for agriculture.

The Botmaskop Fynbos Estate development currently underway exceeds the 2006 footprint 9.4 times, with each one of the 73 stands between 701 square metres to 2735 square metres. They range in price too with the most extensive plot retailing at over R31-million.

The mystery is how the developer did it under the noses of Stellenbosch residents who are fighting the onset of gated estates on all sides of their town. In fact, there are multiple gated estates popping up or planned across the Winelands, aimed to accommodate wealthy and middle class semigres flocking into the Cape, as well as foreigners with cash to burn. A signboard at Pniel shouts to passing motorists: Book your Place in the Winelands Now (maybe not exactly like that, but words to that effect)

In this instance, the developers say their earthmoving is all above board, and they have a piece of paper to prove it, dated 2021. It’s authored by an official in the provincial department of planning and says that the change in the 2006 zoning for a hotel carries through to the environmental impact on the property today, although the project has dramatically changed. This is hard for anybody outside of the development process to believe, watching the bulldozers tear up the mountainside.

There is also a great deal of information that has been hidden from the public in an extensive paper trail of lawyers letters and objections and municipal and provincial assurances. Key amongst the missing documents are:
1) A legal settlement between an earlier developer and the Stellenbosch Municipality over the rezoning for 73 erven in about 2014 which appears to have automatically legalised the rezoning – this has been deemed secret and the municipality has refused to show it to the SIG
2) Any Environmental Assessment for the current development
3) Any Heritage Assessment for the current development
4) Reasons why appeals against the development have been turned down
5) Reasons why appeals against the objections to the land swap been turned down

There is big money at stake at Botmaskop and in the industry of gated estates in the Winelands. This project shows how rezoning agricultural land for a luxury gated estate has dramatically increased the value of the land. In 2003 the 31 hectares land was bought for just over 3 million Rands, ostensibly to develop a hotel for which it engaged in a prolonged public and state approval process. Twenty years later, the current developer, Staytus, buys the same piece of land for R200 million, now with zoning rights. It is bonded for R320 million. It was sold to Staytus by a company called Reset Properties who had bought it in 2017 for R14 million. Reset Properties falls under Foundation Capital which is an office owned by one of South Africa’s wealthiest families, and they were the ones who managed to get the non-substantive amendment passed in the provincial department of the Environmental Department.

At the heart of this dispute are two conflicting visions over the future of Stellenbosch and the Winelands. One group – the wealthy property developers and their friends – want to create a safe space for the very rich, in the beautiful setting of the Winelands, through the ongoing building of gated estates, and the complimentary sponsorship of the town’s projects and aesthetic needs. The other would like to see Stellenbosch develop more slowly, where there is greater integration of the different economic groups, and the town develops sustainably on its own commercial success, respecting the beautiful spaces and agricultural land in which it is set. This is my interpretation after many discussions with people in the area and the town.


Further information:
There are layers and layers of intrigues - here are some of them including unproven rumours

1) The Botmaskop Farm was auctioned very controversially in 2012 to a company called Lancelot Stellenbosch Mountain Retreat. The man behind the holding company was Cobus Kellermann who was accused by Alec Hogg of running the Belvedere Ponzi scheme. It turns out that it wasn’t a Ponzi scheme and Kellermann is sueing Alec Hogg for R5 million but has lost everything including Botmaskop in the process. It’s an extraordinary story – almost worth a Carte Blanche in its own right. But I don’t think it has bearing on this story if it is to be told in 10-12 minutes.
2) The developer, Werner Roux, has a very bad reputation as a person who bulldozes communities in order to get his developments through. He has been involved in a twenty year battle over the development of a site near George at the Maalgat River Mouth which he wanted to turn into two golf estates, and then into a sort of agricultural gentleman’s estate Utopia. A handful of locals have fought him tooth and nail all the way to the Constitutional Court and the matter is not yet resolved. However, it is suggested that he used his political connections to get approvals through the Agricultural Department and also petrol bomb a house of one of the opponents and loosen the screws of a BMW, as well as deliver a death threat in colloquial Afrikaans. Again, this does not have huge bearing on the story at hand. He has done and is busy with multiple projects in the Winelands.
3) There are plenty of rumours swirling around the Botmaskop development, which are juicy but not necessarily material because they can not be proven:
a) That the development is in trouble financially and it has a silent, wealthy funder called Dennis Venter in Somerset West
b) That a Russian or Russians have snapped up a few plots
c) That the Municipal manager has got herself a plot behind the scenes

Press Release:


The Botmaskop Bonanza
A half-hour walk up the mountain above Unie Park in Stellenbosch takes you to a huge construction site, where ground has been broken for what is meant to be one of the Cape's new exclusive lifestyle estates. Roads have been laid on the steep slope and reinforced to prevent erosion, alien plants have been cleared, and the entire area enclosed with a fence which snakes down the mountainside. Luxury houses will go up here, commanding breathtaking views. The developers are selling plots for millions, attracting both local and international buyers who want a taste of the high-end Winelands lifestyle. But for Stellenbosch residents concerned with urban heritage, this development feels very different from the small mountain resort they approved in a 2003 public participation process. And people living in neighbouring Ida’s Valley are chafing at a controversial land swap which they allege favours the developers with a sliver of municipal land in exchange for steep ground on which the developer cannot build. This at a time when plans for social housing on an adjacent piece of land seem to have fallen off the table. Carte Blanche examines the paper trail which throws light and shade on the convoluted process of environmental authorisation for an exclusive housing estate.

THERE’S A BATTLE QUIETLY RAGING IN THE SHADOW OF STELLENBOSCH’S ICONIC MOUNTAINS…
AND IT’S PITTING A FRAGILE ECOSYSTEM AGAINST POWERFUL DEVELOPERS

Brian Du Preez: There's a high likelihood that at least one threatened species has been lost in that development area.

IN THE HEART OF THE CAPE WINELANDS, ANOTHER LUXURY ESTATE IS RISING….
BUT AT WHAT COST?
THE LAND WHICH IS PART OF ONE OF THE WORLD’S RECOGNISED FLORAL KINGDOMS IS BEING TRANSFORMED INTO EXCLUSIVE PROPERTIES FOR THE ULTRA-RICH.
LOCALS FEAR THIS DEVELOPMENT IS A SIGN OF THINGS TO COME.

Werner Roux: There’s a letter from the municipality which states on record that there were no objections.

VO (3) BUT AS THE PAPER TRAIL UNRAVELS, A DIFFERENT STORY EMERGES…ONE OF ALLEGATIONS OF SECRECY, SOARING LAND PRICES AND A COMMUNITY’S GROWING FRUSTRATION

Pieter Schaafsma: He washed his hands of the situation and said: You are too late.

VO (4)
WHO REALLY PROFITS FROM DEVELOPMENT IN THE WINELANDS - AND WHO STANDS TO LOSE?


Allison Smith: My kinders, hulle sal dit nooit kan bekostig nie.
My children won’t be able to afford it.

VO (5)
THIS IS THE STORY OF BOTMASKOP. A STORY OF VULNERABLE BEAUTY RIGHT ON THE EDGE OF ONE OF SOUTH AFRICA’S MOST SOUGHT-AFTER TOWNS, STELLENBOSCH

GOVAN WHITTLES PTC: Some have described Stellenbosch as the crown jewel of the Western Cape with its clean streets and manicured flower beds. So it's not surprising that it's become a prime destination for the super wealthy who want to live a Winelands lifestyle.


(VO 6)
SO PROPERTY DEVELOPERS ARE ON THE PROWL HERE FOR OPPORTUNITIES - MOST NOTABLY GATED LIFESTYLE ESTATES.

AND POSSIBLY THE MOST EXTRAORDINARY OF THESE VENTURES IS BOTMASKOP ESTATE, RIGHT ON THE TOWN’s URBAN EDGE.

THE DEVELOPMENT HAS COME AS A SHOCK TO SOME LOCALS, LIKE BOTANIST BRIAN DU PREEZ.

HE WALKS IN THIS FOREST WEEKLY, LOOKING OUT FOR SPECIAL PLANTS.

Brian du Preez: It’s just over here. This is the Cape Winelands Satin flower,

Govan Whittles: So is this an indigenous plant?

Brian du Preez: This is indigenous and endemic, actually, to the Cape Winelands, one of three endangered species that I've already found growing just randomly in the pine trees here on Botmaskop.

Brian du Preez: This is Botmaskop here…

VO (7)
WE WALKED A FEW METRES FURTHER - AND BEHOLD - A LARGE CONSTRUCTION SITE….

Govan Whittles: Oh, wow.

WITH BREATHTAKING VIEWS.

Govan Whittles: So this is it hey.

Brian du Preez: This is part of it.

VO (8) ONCE A FARM, THE LAND IS NOW DESTINED TO BE AN EXCLUSIVE ESTATE.

Govan Whittles: Yo, it looks precarious.

Brian du Preez: I don't know. They're gonna do some balancing act here to to get some houses up.

BRIAN DU PREEZ
Botanist
The first thing I did was I tried to find out, where is the environmental impact assessment? These documents are supposed to be available publicly, and just couldn't no way find anything. So started digging a little bit deeper.

VO (09) STELLENBOSCH RESIDENTS HAVE BEEN TRACKING PLANS FOR THIS PROPERTY FOR TWO DECADES.
THEY HAD SUPPORTED AN INITIAL DEVELOPMENT TWENTY YEARS AGO, AFTER AN ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT WAS DONE in 2003 - BUT NOT THIS.

GOVAN WHITTLES PTC: Originally, approval was granted to build a small mountain resort here. It would have a hotel with 10 rooms and 15 chalets, but that was never built.

VO (10 )PIETER SCHAAFSMA, A RETIRED TOWN PLANNER, WAS CAUGHT OFF GUARD.

Pieter Schaafsma: This is municipal land and this is the issue here.

VO (11 ) PIETER IS FROM THE STELLENBOSCH INTEREST GROUP OR SIG. IT’S A GROUP OF LOCAL ACTIVISTS WHO ENGAGE WITH THE MUNICIPALITY ON LAND USE APPLICATIONS, AND THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT WHICH OVERSEES ENVIRONMENTAL APPROVALS.

Pieter Schaafsma: People around town said, Oh, Peter, you're on the committee there. What the hell is going on at Botmaskop?

(VO12) BUT THE BULLDOZERS WERE ALREADY CARVING UP THE LAND INTO 77 ERVEN
AND SIG’S APPLICATION FOR PERMISSION TO LODGE A LATE APPEAL TO THE TO THE RESPONSIBLE PROVINCIAL MINISTER ANTON BREDELL WAS DENIED.

Govan Whittles: Why were the people never informed?
Pieter Schaafsma: Reasons were asked for and never provided. The answer was: we must take it to the High Court.

Brian du Preez: It was only after I started snooping around here that they started putting up fences and gates. But yeah, it's all happened very, very, very fast.

GOVAN WHITTLES PIECE TO CAM: There's a long and complex paper trail concerning this property that stretches from the top of Botmaskop all the way to the mayor's office. It's a cat and mouse game involving development rights and zoning.

VO) (13) THE STELLENBOSCH MUNICIPAL MANAGER, GERALDINE METTLER, SAYS THE DEVELOPMENT IS A DONE DEAL.

Govan Whittles: You know some Stellenbosch residents call it a scar on the mountain.

Geraldine Mettler: Yeah, they can but probably it’s a perception issue… people don't tend to understand that a town that doesn't develop dies. You need to develop in order to create those access and services and cross subsidization that you so much require. Who is going to pay for that?

GOVAN TRIES TO SAY SOMETHING: The problem -

Geraldine Mettler: But no wait, the key here is to make sure that whatever you develop: is it sustainable? And that it doesn’t have a negative impact on the environment. The question is how do I deal with the hand that I have been dealt with in a manner that is beneficial to everybody.

Govan Whittles: Are you under pressure right now?

Geraldine Mettler: No. I don't see it as being under pressure. I have a council policy, and my council policy is what we called spatial development framework.

Govan Whittles: But the property developers can be fierce lobbyists?

Geraldine Mettler: … they can lobby as much as they like, it depends on who you talk to. If you are going to speak to the developer, they are going to tell you I’m a witch.

Govan Whittles: and if I speak to the community?

Geraldine Mettler: They are going to also tell you I’m a witch.

VO (14) ACROSS THE ROAD TO THE ENTRANCE OF THE ESTATE IS ONE OF STELLENBOSCH’S OLDEST SUBURBS, IDA’S VALLEY.
BUT THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE HERE ARE ON A WAITING LIST FOR SOCIAL HOUSING.
RESIDENT ALLISON SMITH AND HER NEIGHBOURS ARE WORRIED ABOUT THE FUTURE OF THE COMMUNITY.

Allison Smith: Om hier te bly, of in so tipe huis to bly. My kinders sal dit nie kan bekostig nie.

SUBTITLE: To live here, to live in a house like this, my children won’t be able to afford that.

Allison Smith: Weet jy hoeveel mense hierso, die jeug, is unemployed, daar’ is net niks, daar is nie werk nie, en op die einde van die dag kos dit, jy moet maar ‘n hokkie gaan opsit.

SUBTITLE: Do you now how many people, the youth, are unemployed. There is just nothing for them, there is no work, and at the end of the day, you just have to put up a shack.

(VO15) THE DEVELOPMENT OF A LUXURY ESTATE ON THEIR DOORSTEP IS SALT IN THE WOUNDS. THIS GROUP REMEMBER THAT IDA’S VALLEY USED TO STRETCH OVER THE HELSHOOGTE ROAD IN EARLIER TIMES.

Abraham Moses: Dit was alles Idasvallei.

SUBITITLE: This was all Ida’s Valley.

Govan Whittles: Hier wat did beplanning…

SUBITITLE: Here were the plans…

Abraham Moses: Dit was alles Idasvallei. Die pad het die skeiding kom maak.

SUBITITLE: This was all Ida’s Valley. The road came and made the division.

(VO16)THESE IDA’s VALLEY RESIDENTS SAY THAT MORE RECENTLY THE MUNICIPALITY HAD CONSIDERED LAND THERE FOR SOCIAL AND LOW-COST HOUSING.


Allison Smith: Ja, daar’s groot verwagtinge.

SUBITITLE: There are high expectations.

Govan Whittles: Vir huise op die Botmaskop?

SUBITITLE: For houses on Botmaskop?

Allison Smith:
Vir huise ja. Dis mos nou belofte wat gemaak was oor die jare deur die municipalitet.

SUBITITLE: Yes, for houses.
This was a promise made by the municipality over the years.

So dit is hoekom ons mense ok mos nie uitbeweeg hierdie area uit nie.
So that is why our people are not moving out of the area.

SUBITITLE: So that is why our people are not moving out of the area.

Hulle hou vas hierso, and en dit is waar ons gebore is. …

SUBITITLE: The are digging in here and this is where we were born….

En dit is hoekom hulle daai verwagting het dat hier laerkoste behuising of middelklas behuising gebou kan word.

SUBITITLE: And that is why they have that expectation, that low-cost of middle class housing can be built here.

(VO17) THIS PLAN SEEMS NOW TO BE OFF THE TABLE.
METTLER CONCEDED THAT A FEASIBILITY PLAN FOR SOCIAL HOUSING WAS DONE ON AN ADJACENT PIECE OF GROUND WHICH HAD ALSO GONE BY THE NAME OF BOTMASKOP, POSSIBLY CREATING CONFUSION.

Geraldine Mettler: I think there is a a bit of a misunderstanding there.

Govan Whittles: and people we've spoken to recall those meetings with the municipality.

Geraldine Mettler: Well, I wasn't privy to those meetings.

VO (18)
SOME IN THE COMMUNITY ARE ALSO ANGRY OVER A CONTROVERSIAL LAND SWAP BETWEEN BOTMASKOP ESTATE AND THE MUNICIPALITY EARLIER THIS YEAR.
IN EXCHANGE FOR 4-AND-A HALF HECTARES OF VERY STEEP SLOPE, THE DEVELOPERS ARE GAINING A BUFFER SLICED OUT OF MUNICIPAL LAND ON THEIR TOP BOUNDARY.

Govan Whittles: What you got was a steep hill with bicycle trails on it.

Geraldine Mettler: Yes, with access to the entire Stellenbosch Community

Govan Whittles: And you say that's worth exactly the same amount as a piece of land right on the border where they're building an estate worth hundreds of millions of
Rands.

Geraldine Mettler: Yes, I am saying that because they will never be able to develop there.

VO (19)
LOCAL COUNCILLOR, MARIUS VAN STADE, SAYS THE LAND SWAP WAS PUSHED THROUGH COUNCIL WITHOUT PROPER PUBLIC CONSULTATION - A CHARGE THE MUNICIPAL MANAGER DENIES.

Marius van Stade: In terms of the motivation given to us in Council for the land swap, they indicated to us that the land of the property, the private property developer, is of the same value and market value of the municipal land, which is untrue, because the land of the property developer is laying in a ditch downhill, while the two land parcels of Stellenbosch Municipality was was on top of the hill with a nice view …even with a view to Cape Town as well.


(VO 20) THE BOTMASKOP LAND PRICE HAS SURGED SINCE THE PLAN TO TURN IT INTO A RESIDENTIAL ESTATE TOOK SHAPE, ALTHOUGH A PREVIOUS OWNER SAYS THAT THE PURCHASE PRICES RECORDED AT THE DEEDS OFFICE DID NOT ALWAYS REFLECT THE ACTUAL LAND VALUES OF THE TIME, NOR THE ACQUISITION COSTS.

GOVAN WHITTLES PTC: This piece of mountainside was bought in 2003 for just over 3 million Rand. It changed hands, and then in 2017 it was sold for 14 million Rand. Five years later, it was sold again, this time for 200 million Rand.

(VO 21) THE NEW OWNERS, PROPERTY DEVELOPERS, WERNER ROUX, AND HANDRE BASSON SAY THEY ARE REHABILITATING THE SITE, PLANTING INDIGENOUS VEGETATION.
DESPITE THE BAD WEATHER, WERNER SHOWED US HOW THEIR PLANS WERE TAKING SHAPE ON THE MOUNTAINSIDE.

Govan Whittles: It’s a pity about the rain…. These are steep slopes.

Werner Roux: Especially during the rainy season. It was very challenging.
But Govan, that is what it looked like. Look at that side of the valley, and on the top there you can see that is the municipal land where there are no alien trees and just indigenous fynbos.So that is how we inherited the site, full of these alien trees.

(VO 22) WERNER INTRODUCED US TO A BUYER, PIETER BRUNDYN, AN EXPERIENCED PROPERTY ENTREPRENEUR FROM OUT OF TOWN.

Pieter Brundyn: We come here as a on a weekend, or we come for restaurants, or we come for lifestyle. … it was just look, firstly, I made an investment decision to say, I think it's a good investment. And then you bring in lifestyle,

Govan Whittles: Can you say how much you paid for the plot?

Pieter Brundyn: Too much, too little. You know, the right price somewhere there in the middle is the right answer.

Govan Whittles: Was this an expensive buy. That's what I'm asking

Pieter Brundyn: For Stellenbosch, I think it is expensive buy,

(VO 23) PRICES IN THE CATALOGUE SHOW PLOTS RANGE FROM R4 TO UP TO R30 MILLION. WERNER AND HIS PARTNER HAVE BOUGHT A PLOT THEMSELVES.

Govan Whittles: Can you talk about who is buying?

Werner Roux: We've had some Europeans that have bought..

Govan Whittles: Some Russians?

Werner Roux: Some Russians have bought, but the bulk of the buyers are South Africans.

(VO 24) AND ACCORDING TO WERNER, GATED ESTATES ARE EXACTLY WHAT THE MARKET WANTS.

WERNER ROUX
Property Developer, STAYTUS
Bear in mind that a lot of the people that are relocating to the Cape are all ex Gauteng people. Those people are very concerned, and they are very risk averse, and therefore they insist and they will only buy in gated estates.

Govan Whittles: How difficult is it to get the authority to go ahead with such a development when there are groups actively pushing against it?

Werner Roux: In terms of our process and the final approvals, I'll show you that there were no objections to our application, and I've got it in writing here to show you.

Govan Whittles: What is the date on that Environmental Impact Assessment Approval?

Werner Roux: 2021

Govan Whittles: 2021

(VO 25) IN TRACKING THE STEPS THAT LED TO THAT 2021 APPROVAL, WE ESTABLISHED THAT A PUBLIC PARTICIPATION PROCESS WAS STARTED - AND THEN SCRAPPED.

Pieter Schaafsma: And that's where the application to develop just vanished
It means that there was no further feedback from the environmental practitioner who had registered the interest group as an interested and affected parties.

Govan Whittles: But the plans to develop didn't stop.

Pieter Schaafsma: Well, behind the scenes, things were happening.

(VO26) THE NEXT THING PIETER KNEW WAS THAT THE LAND HAD BEEN SOLD.
AND THE ORIGINAL ENVIRONMENTAL AUTHORISATION FOR A RESORT IN 2003, NOW AMENDED, WAS THE TICKET TO BUILD.

Pieter Schaafsma: Ja that was a different concept, that is like chalets and accessible to the broader community, this is a sterile piece of land for the super-rich.

(VO)27 ESSENTIALLY THE DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS AND PLANNING HAD GIVEN ITS APPROVAL TO THE RESIDENTIAL ESTATE WITHOUT THE DEVELOPERS HAVING TO ENGAGE IN A NEW ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT, NOR CANVAS PUBLIC OPINION AGAIN.

Govan Whittles: Was there any other environmental impact assessment done that you've seen after the change was made to develop a residential property?

Werner Roux: I honestly can't tell you.

(VO 27)
IT’S NOW THE ELEVENTH HOUR - BUT THE STELLENBOSCH INTEREST GROUP HAS NOT YET GIVEN UP THE FIGHT.

Pieter Schaafsma: The buildings are yet to come. And you know when people pay up to 25 million for a plot. They're not going to put a Pondok on there. There's going to be a big structure there.

Summary: An half an hour walk up the mountain above Unie Park in Stellenbosch takes you to the top of the Botmaskop Fynbos Estate, which is under construction. Roads have been laid on the steep slope, and reinforced to prevent erosion, and an expensive clearvu fence erected, which I was told had been paid for by the municipality, to keep the public out. A reservoir has been erected at the top as well, which the environmentalists claim was done so illegally. On their website the developers claim that this is the highest residential estate ever approved above sea level – almost 400 metres. But the question is this: Was it ever properly approved? Or has the rezoning of this development, and a subsequent landswap with the municipality to change its boundaries, been a sleight of hand? There are no boards on the gate which indicate which, if any Environmental Company has done the assessment in anticipation of approval. The property was bought and zoned in 2006 for a small mountain retreat which would be 15 chalets not exceeding 400m² each, so 6000m² of development as well as a hotel with 10 rooms not exceeding 2800m² . The rest of the 30 hectare property was zoned for agriculture. The Botmaskop Fynbos Estate development currently underway exceeds the 2006 footprint 9.4 times, with each one of the 73 stands between 701 square metres to 2735 square metres. They range in price too with the most extensive plot retailing at over R31-million. The mystery is how the developer did it under the noses of Stellenbosch residents who are fighting the onset of gated estates on all sides of their town. In fact, there are multiple gated estates popping up or planned across the Winelands, aimed to accommodate wealthy and middle class semigres flocking into the Cape, as well as foreigners with cash to burn. A signboard at Pniel shouts to passing motorists: Book your Place in the Winelands Now (maybe not exactly like that, but words to that effect) In this instance, the developers say their earthmoving is all above board, and they have a piece of paper to prove it, dated 2021. It’s authored by an official in the provincial department of planning and says that the change in the 2006 zoning for a hotel carries through to the environmental impact on the property today, although the project has dramatically changed. This is hard for anybody outside of the development process to believe, watching the bulldozers tear up the mountainside. There is also a great deal of information that has been hidden from the public in an extensive paper trail of lawyers letters and objections and municipal and provincial assurances. Key amongst the missing documents are: 1) A legal settlement between an earlier developer and the Stellenbosch Municipality over the rezoning for 73 erven in about 2014 which appears to have automatically legalised the rezoning – this has been deemed secret and the municipality has refused to show it to the SIG 2) Any Environmental Assessment for the current development 3) Any Heritage Assessment for the current development 4) Reasons why appeals against the development have been turned down 5) Reasons why appeals against the objections to the land swap been turned down There is big money at stake at Botmaskop and in the industry of gated estates in the Winelands. This project shows how rezoning agricultural land for a luxury gated estate has dramatically increased the value of the land. In 2003 the 31 hectares land was bought for just over 3 million Rands, ostensibly to develop a hotel for which it engaged in a prolonged public and state approval process. Twenty years later, the current developer, Staytus, buys the same piece of land for R200 million, now with zoning rights. It is bonded for R320 million. It was sold to Staytus by a company called Reset Properties who had bought it in 2017 for R14 million. Reset Properties falls under Foundation Capital which is an office owned by one of South Africa’s wealthiest families, and they were the ones who managed to get the non-substantive amendment passed in the provincial department of the Environmental Department. At the heart of this dispute are two conflicting visions over the future of Stellenbosch and the Winelands. One group – the wealthy property developers and their friends – want to create a safe space for the very rich, in the beautiful setting of the Winelands, through the ongoing building of gated estates, and the complimentary sponsorship of the town’s projects and aesthetic needs. The other would like to see Stellenbosch develop more slowly, where there is greater integration of the different economic groups, and the town develops sustainably on its own commercial success, respecting the beautiful spaces and agricultural land in which it is set. This is my interpretation after many discussions with people in the area and the town. Further information: There are layers and layers of intrigues - here are some of them including unproven rumours 1) The Botmaskop Farm was auctioned very controversially in 2012 to a company called Lancelot Stellenbosch Mountain Retreat. The man behind the holding company was Cobus Kellermann who was accused by Alec Hogg of running the Belvedere Ponzi scheme. It turns out that it wasn’t a Ponzi scheme and Kellermann is sueing Alec Hogg for R5 million but has lost everything including Botmaskop in the process. It’s an extraordinary story – almost worth a Carte Blanche in its own right. But I don’t think it has bearing on this story if it is to be told in 10-12 minutes. 2) The developer, Werner Roux, has a very bad reputation as a person who bulldozes communities in order to get his developments through. He has been involved in a twenty year battle over the development of a site near George at the Maalgat River Mouth which he wanted to turn into two golf estates, and then into a sort of agricultural gentleman’s estate Utopia. A handful of locals have fought him tooth and nail all the way to the Constitutional Court and the matter is not yet resolved. However, it is suggested that he used his political connections to get approvals through the Agricultural Department and also petrol bomb a house of one of the opponents and loosen the screws of a BMW, as well as deliver a death threat in colloquial Afrikaans. Again, this does not have huge bearing on the story at hand. He has done and is busy with multiple projects in the Winelands. 3) There are plenty of rumours swirling around the Botmaskop development, which are juicy but not necessarily material because they can not be proven: a) That the development is in trouble financially and it has a silent, wealthy funder called Dennis Venter in Somerset West b) That a Russian or Russians have snapped up a few plots c) That the Municipal manager has got herself a plot behind the scenes Case Study: Brian Du Preez Pieter Schaarfsma Marius Van Stade Allison Smith Expert: Geraldine Mettler Werner Roux Locations: Stellenbosch Hidden Camera: No Legal: Yes Reason for legal: This is a complex story which involves litigious and bully boy property developers Graphics: Yes Reason for graphics: We might need them to show where Botmaskop is. mihle@combinedartists.co.za 06 October 2024 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: The Botmaskop Bonanza A half-hour walk up the mountain above Unie Park in Stellenbosch takes you to a huge construction site, where ground has been broken for what is meant to be one of the Cape's new exclusive lifestyle estates. Roads have been laid on the steep slope and reinforced to prevent erosion, alien plants have been cleared, and the entire area enclosed with a fence which snakes down the mountainside. Luxury houses will go up here, commanding breathtaking views. The developers are selling plots for millions, attracting both local and international buyers who want a taste of the high-end Winelands lifestyle. But for Stellenbosch residents concerned with urban heritage, this development feels very different from the small mountain resort they approved in a 2003 public participation process. And people living in neighbouring Ida’s Valley are chafing at a controversial land swap which they allege favours the developers with a sliver of municipal land in exchange for steep ground on which the developer cannot build. This at a time when plans for social housing on an adjacent piece of land seem to have fallen off the table. Carte Blanche examines the paper trail which throws light and shade on the convoluted process of environmental authorisation for an exclusive housing estate. Script: VO (1) THERE’S A BATTLE QUIETLY RAGING IN THE SHADOW OF STELLENBOSCH’S ICONIC MOUNTAINS… AND IT’S PITTING A FRAGILE ECOSYSTEM AGAINST POWERFUL DEVELOPERS Brian Du Preez: There's a high likelihood that at least one threatened species has been lost in that development area. VO (2) IN THE HEART OF THE CAPE WINELANDS, ANOTHER LUXURY ESTATE IS RISING…. BUT AT WHAT COST? THE LAND WHICH IS PART OF ONE OF THE WORLD’S RECOGNISED FLORAL KINGDOMS IS BEING TRANSFORMED INTO EXCLUSIVE PROPERTIES FOR THE ULTRA-RICH. LOCALS FEAR THIS DEVELOPMENT IS A SIGN OF THINGS TO COME. Werner Roux: There’s a letter from the municipality which states on record that there were no objections. VO (3) BUT AS THE PAPER TRAIL UNRAVELS, A DIFFERENT STORY EMERGES…ONE OF ALLEGATIONS OF SECRECY, SOARING LAND PRICES AND A COMMUNITY’S GROWING FRUSTRATION Pieter Schaafsma: He washed his hands of the situation and said: You are too late. VO (4) WHO REALLY PROFITS FROM DEVELOPMENT IN THE WINELANDS - AND WHO STANDS TO LOSE? Allison Smith: My kinders, hulle sal dit nooit kan bekostig nie. My children won’t be able to afford it. VO (5) THIS IS THE STORY OF BOTMASKOP. A STORY OF VULNERABLE BEAUTY RIGHT ON THE EDGE OF ONE OF SOUTH AFRICA’S MOST SOUGHT-AFTER TOWNS, STELLENBOSCH GOVAN WHITTLES PTC: Some have described Stellenbosch as the crown jewel of the Western Cape with its clean streets and manicured flower beds. So it's not surprising that it's become a prime destination for the super wealthy who want to live a Winelands lifestyle. (VO 6) SO PROPERTY DEVELOPERS ARE ON THE PROWL HERE FOR OPPORTUNITIES - MOST NOTABLY GATED LIFESTYLE ESTATES. AND POSSIBLY THE MOST EXTRAORDINARY OF THESE VENTURES IS BOTMASKOP ESTATE, RIGHT ON THE TOWN’s URBAN EDGE. THE DEVELOPMENT HAS COME AS A SHOCK TO SOME LOCALS, LIKE BOTANIST BRIAN DU PREEZ. HE WALKS IN THIS FOREST WEEKLY, LOOKING OUT FOR SPECIAL PLANTS. Brian du Preez: It’s just over here. This is the Cape Winelands Satin flower, Govan Whittles: So is this an indigenous plant? Brian du Preez: This is indigenous and endemic, actually, to the Cape Winelands, one of three endangered species that I've already found growing just randomly in the pine trees here on Botmaskop. Brian du Preez: This is Botmaskop here… VO (7) WE WALKED A FEW METRES FURTHER - AND BEHOLD - A LARGE CONSTRUCTION SITE…. Govan Whittles: Oh, wow. WITH BREATHTAKING VIEWS. Govan Whittles: So this is it hey. Brian du Preez: This is part of it. VO (8) ONCE A FARM, THE LAND IS NOW DESTINED TO BE AN EXCLUSIVE ESTATE. Govan Whittles: Yo, it looks precarious. Brian du Preez: I don't know. They're gonna do some balancing act here to to get some houses up. BRIAN DU PREEZ Botanist The first thing I did was I tried to find out, where is the environmental impact assessment? These documents are supposed to be available publicly, and just couldn't no way find anything. So started digging a little bit deeper. VO (09) STELLENBOSCH RESIDENTS HAVE BEEN TRACKING PLANS FOR THIS PROPERTY FOR TWO DECADES. THEY HAD SUPPORTED AN INITIAL DEVELOPMENT TWENTY YEARS AGO, AFTER AN ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT WAS DONE in 2003 - BUT NOT THIS. GOVAN WHITTLES PTC: Originally, approval was granted to build a small mountain resort here. It would have a hotel with 10 rooms and 15 chalets, but that was never built. VO (10 )PIETER SCHAAFSMA, A RETIRED TOWN PLANNER, WAS CAUGHT OFF GUARD. Pieter Schaafsma: This is municipal land and this is the issue here. VO (11 ) PIETER IS FROM THE STELLENBOSCH INTEREST GROUP OR SIG. IT’S A GROUP OF LOCAL ACTIVISTS WHO ENGAGE WITH THE MUNICIPALITY ON LAND USE APPLICATIONS, AND THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT WHICH OVERSEES ENVIRONMENTAL APPROVALS. Pieter Schaafsma: People around town said, Oh, Peter, you're on the committee there. What the hell is going on at Botmaskop? (VO12) BUT THE BULLDOZERS WERE ALREADY CARVING UP THE LAND INTO 77 ERVEN AND SIG’S APPLICATION FOR PERMISSION TO LODGE A LATE APPEAL TO THE TO THE RESPONSIBLE PROVINCIAL MINISTER ANTON BREDELL WAS DENIED. Govan Whittles: Why were the people never informed? Pieter Schaafsma: Reasons were asked for and never provided. The answer was: we must take it to the High Court. Brian du Preez: It was only after I started snooping around here that they started putting up fences and gates. But yeah, it's all happened very, very, very fast. GOVAN WHITTLES PIECE TO CAM: There's a long and complex paper trail concerning this property that stretches from the top of Botmaskop all the way to the mayor's office. It's a cat and mouse game involving development rights and zoning. VO) (13) THE STELLENBOSCH MUNICIPAL MANAGER, GERALDINE METTLER, SAYS THE DEVELOPMENT IS A DONE DEAL. Govan Whittles: You know some Stellenbosch residents call it a scar on the mountain. Geraldine Mettler: Yeah, they can but probably it’s a perception issue… people don't tend to understand that a town that doesn't develop dies. You need to develop in order to create those access and services and cross subsidization that you so much require. Who is going to pay for that? GOVAN TRIES TO SAY SOMETHING: The problem - Geraldine Mettler: But no wait, the key here is to make sure that whatever you develop: is it sustainable? And that it doesn’t have a negative impact on the environment. The question is how do I deal with the hand that I have been dealt with in a manner that is beneficial to everybody. Govan Whittles: Are you under pressure right now? Geraldine Mettler: No. I don't see it as being under pressure. I have a council policy, and my council policy is what we called spatial development framework. Govan Whittles: But the property developers can be fierce lobbyists? Geraldine Mettler: … they can lobby as much as they like, it depends on who you talk to. If you are going to speak to the developer, they are going to tell you I’m a witch. Govan Whittles: and if I speak to the community? Geraldine Mettler: They are going to also tell you I’m a witch. VO (14) ACROSS THE ROAD TO THE ENTRANCE OF THE ESTATE IS ONE OF STELLENBOSCH’S OLDEST SUBURBS, IDA’S VALLEY. BUT THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE HERE ARE ON A WAITING LIST FOR SOCIAL HOUSING. RESIDENT ALLISON SMITH AND HER NEIGHBOURS ARE WORRIED ABOUT THE FUTURE OF THE COMMUNITY. Allison Smith: Om hier te bly, of in so tipe huis to bly. My kinders sal dit nie kan bekostig nie. SUBTITLE: To live here, to live in a house like this, my children won’t be able to afford that. Allison Smith: Weet jy hoeveel mense hierso, die jeug, is unemployed, daar’ is net niks, daar is nie werk nie, en op die einde van die dag kos dit, jy moet maar ‘n hokkie gaan opsit. SUBTITLE: Do you now how many people, the youth, are unemployed. There is just nothing for them, there is no work, and at the end of the day, you just have to put up a shack. (VO15) THE DEVELOPMENT OF A LUXURY ESTATE ON THEIR DOORSTEP IS SALT IN THE WOUNDS. THIS GROUP REMEMBER THAT IDA’S VALLEY USED TO STRETCH OVER THE HELSHOOGTE ROAD IN EARLIER TIMES. Abraham Moses: Dit was alles Idasvallei. SUBITITLE: This was all Ida’s Valley. Govan Whittles: Hier wat did beplanning… SUBITITLE: Here were the plans… Abraham Moses: Dit was alles Idasvallei. Die pad het die skeiding kom maak. SUBITITLE: This was all Ida’s Valley. The road came and made the division. (VO16)THESE IDA’s VALLEY RESIDENTS SAY THAT MORE RECENTLY THE MUNICIPALITY HAD CONSIDERED LAND THERE FOR SOCIAL AND LOW-COST HOUSING. Allison Smith: Ja, daar’s groot verwagtinge. SUBITITLE: There are high expectations. Govan Whittles: Vir huise op die Botmaskop? SUBITITLE: For houses on Botmaskop? Allison Smith: Vir huise ja. Dis mos nou belofte wat gemaak was oor die jare deur die municipalitet. SUBITITLE: Yes, for houses. This was a promise made by the municipality over the years. So dit is hoekom ons mense ok mos nie uitbeweeg hierdie area uit nie. So that is why our people are not moving out of the area. SUBITITLE: So that is why our people are not moving out of the area. Hulle hou vas hierso, and en dit is waar ons gebore is. … SUBITITLE: The are digging in here and this is where we were born…. En dit is hoekom hulle daai verwagting het dat hier laerkoste behuising of middelklas behuising gebou kan word. SUBITITLE: And that is why they have that expectation, that low-cost of middle class housing can be built here. (VO17) THIS PLAN SEEMS NOW TO BE OFF THE TABLE. METTLER CONCEDED THAT A FEASIBILITY PLAN FOR SOCIAL HOUSING WAS DONE ON AN ADJACENT PIECE OF GROUND WHICH HAD ALSO GONE BY THE NAME OF BOTMASKOP, POSSIBLY CREATING CONFUSION. Geraldine Mettler: I think there is a a bit of a misunderstanding there. Govan Whittles: and people we've spoken to recall those meetings with the municipality. Geraldine Mettler: Well, I wasn't privy to those meetings. VO (18) SOME IN THE COMMUNITY ARE ALSO ANGRY OVER A CONTROVERSIAL LAND SWAP BETWEEN BOTMASKOP ESTATE AND THE MUNICIPALITY EARLIER THIS YEAR. IN EXCHANGE FOR 4-AND-A HALF HECTARES OF VERY STEEP SLOPE, THE DEVELOPERS ARE GAINING A BUFFER SLICED OUT OF MUNICIPAL LAND ON THEIR TOP BOUNDARY. Govan Whittles: What you got was a steep hill with bicycle trails on it. Geraldine Mettler: Yes, with access to the entire Stellenbosch Community Govan Whittles: And you say that's worth exactly the same amount as a piece of land right on the border where they're building an estate worth hundreds of millions of Rands. Geraldine Mettler: Yes, I am saying that because they will never be able to develop there. VO (19) LOCAL COUNCILLOR, MARIUS VAN STADE, SAYS THE LAND SWAP WAS PUSHED THROUGH COUNCIL WITHOUT PROPER PUBLIC CONSULTATION - A CHARGE THE MUNICIPAL MANAGER DENIES. Marius van Stade: In terms of the motivation given to us in Council for the land swap, they indicated to us that the land of the property, the private property developer, is of the same value and market value of the municipal land, which is untrue, because the land of the property developer is laying in a ditch downhill, while the two land parcels of Stellenbosch Municipality was was on top of the hill with a nice view …even with a view to Cape Town as well. (VO 20) THE BOTMASKOP LAND PRICE HAS SURGED SINCE THE PLAN TO TURN IT INTO A RESIDENTIAL ESTATE TOOK SHAPE, ALTHOUGH A PREVIOUS OWNER SAYS THAT THE PURCHASE PRICES RECORDED AT THE DEEDS OFFICE DID NOT ALWAYS REFLECT THE ACTUAL LAND VALUES OF THE TIME, NOR THE ACQUISITION COSTS. GOVAN WHITTLES PTC: This piece of mountainside was bought in 2003 for just over 3 million Rand. It changed hands, and then in 2017 it was sold for 14 million Rand. Five years later, it was sold again, this time for 200 million Rand. (VO 21) THE NEW OWNERS, PROPERTY DEVELOPERS, WERNER ROUX, AND HANDRE BASSON SAY THEY ARE REHABILITATING THE SITE, PLANTING INDIGENOUS VEGETATION. DESPITE THE BAD WEATHER, WERNER SHOWED US HOW THEIR PLANS WERE TAKING SHAPE ON THE MOUNTAINSIDE. Govan Whittles: It’s a pity about the rain…. These are steep slopes. Werner Roux: Especially during the rainy season. It was very challenging. But Govan, that is what it looked like. Look at that side of the valley, and on the top there you can see that is the municipal land where there are no alien trees and just indigenous fynbos.So that is how we inherited the site, full of these alien trees. (VO 22) WERNER INTRODUCED US TO A BUYER, PIETER BRUNDYN, AN EXPERIENCED PROPERTY ENTREPRENEUR FROM OUT OF TOWN. Pieter Brundyn: We come here as a on a weekend, or we come for restaurants, or we come for lifestyle. … it was just look, firstly, I made an investment decision to say, I think it's a good investment. And then you bring in lifestyle, Govan Whittles: Can you say how much you paid for the plot? Pieter Brundyn: Too much, too little. You know, the right price somewhere there in the middle is the right answer. Govan Whittles: Was this an expensive buy. That's what I'm asking Pieter Brundyn: For Stellenbosch, I think it is expensive buy, (VO 23) PRICES IN THE CATALOGUE SHOW PLOTS RANGE FROM R4 TO UP TO R30 MILLION. WERNER AND HIS PARTNER HAVE BOUGHT A PLOT THEMSELVES. Govan Whittles: Can you talk about who is buying? Werner Roux: We've had some Europeans that have bought.. Govan Whittles: Some Russians? Werner Roux: Some Russians have bought, but the bulk of the buyers are South Africans. (VO 24) AND ACCORDING TO WERNER, GATED ESTATES ARE EXACTLY WHAT THE MARKET WANTS. WERNER ROUX Property Developer, STAYTUS Bear in mind that a lot of the people that are relocating to the Cape are all ex Gauteng people. Those people are very concerned, and they are very risk averse, and therefore they insist and they will only buy in gated estates. Govan Whittles: How difficult is it to get the authority to go ahead with such a development when there are groups actively pushing against it? Werner Roux: In terms of our process and the final approvals, I'll show you that there were no objections to our application, and I've got it in writing here to show you. Govan Whittles: What is the date on that Environmental Impact Assessment Approval? Werner Roux: 2021 Govan Whittles: 2021 (VO 25) IN TRACKING THE STEPS THAT LED TO THAT 2021 APPROVAL, WE ESTABLISHED THAT A PUBLIC PARTICIPATION PROCESS WAS STARTED - AND THEN SCRAPPED. Pieter Schaafsma: And that's where the application to develop just vanished It means that there was no further feedback from the environmental practitioner who had registered the interest group as an interested and affected parties. Govan Whittles: But the plans to develop didn't stop. Pieter Schaafsma: Well, behind the scenes, things were happening. (VO26) THE NEXT THING PIETER KNEW WAS THAT THE LAND HAD BEEN SOLD. AND THE ORIGINAL ENVIRONMENTAL AUTHORISATION FOR A RESORT IN 2003, NOW AMENDED, WAS THE TICKET TO BUILD. Pieter Schaafsma: Ja that was a different concept, that is like chalets and accessible to the broader community, this is a sterile piece of land for the super-rich. (VO)27 ESSENTIALLY THE DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS AND PLANNING HAD GIVEN ITS APPROVAL TO THE RESIDENTIAL ESTATE WITHOUT THE DEVELOPERS HAVING TO ENGAGE IN A NEW ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT, NOR CANVAS PUBLIC OPINION AGAIN. Govan Whittles: Was there any other environmental impact assessment done that you've seen after the change was made to develop a residential property? Werner Roux: I honestly can't tell you. (VO 27) IT’S NOW THE ELEVENTH HOUR - BUT THE STELLENBOSCH INTEREST GROUP HAS NOT YET GIVEN UP THE FIGHT. Pieter Schaafsma: The buildings are yet to come. And you know when people pay up to 25 million for a plot. They're not going to put a Pondok on there. There's going to be a big structure there. A reservoir has been erected at the top as well, which the environmentalists claim was done so illegally. On their website the developers claim that this is the highest residential estate ever approved above sea level – almost 400 metres. But the question is this: Was it ever properly approved? Or has the rezoning of this development, and a subsequent landswap with the municipality to change its boundaries, been a sleight of hand? There are no boards on the gate which indicate which, if any Environmental Company has done the assessment in anticipation of approval. The property was bought and zoned in 2006 for a small mountain retreat which would be 15 chalets not exceeding 400m² each, so 6000m² of development as well as a hotel with 10 rooms not exceeding 2800m² . The rest of the 30 hectare property was zoned for agriculture. The Botmaskop Fynbos Estate development currently underway exceeds the 2006 footprint 9.4 times, with each one of the 73 stands between 701 square metres to 2735 square metres. They range in price too with the most extensive plot retailing at over R31-million. The mystery is how the developer did it under the noses of Stellenbosch residents who are fighting the onset of gated estates on all sides of their town. In fact, there are multiple gated estates popping up or planned across the Winelands, aimed to accommodate wealthy and middle class semigres flocking into the Cape, as well as foreigners with cash to burn. A signboard at Pniel shouts to passing motorists: Book your Place in the Winelands Now (maybe not exactly like that, but words to that effect) In this instance, the developers say their earthmoving is all above board, and they have a piece of paper to prove it, dated 2021. It’s authored by an official in the provincial department of planning and says that the change in the 2006 zoning for a hotel carries through to the environmental impact on the property today, although the project has dramatically changed. This is hard for anybody outside of the development process to believe, watching the bulldozers tear up the mountainside. There is also a great deal of information that has been hidden from the public in an extensive paper trail of lawyers letters and objections and municipal and provincial assurances. Key amongst the missing documents are: 1) A legal settlement between an earlier developer and the Stellenbosch Municipality over the rezoning for 73 erven in about 2014 which appears to have automatically legalised the rezoning – this has been deemed secret and the municipality has refused to show it to the SIG 2) Any Environmental Assessment for the current development 3) Any Heritage Assessment for the current development 4) Reasons why appeals against the development have been turned down 5) Reasons why appeals against the objections to the land swap been turned down There is big money at stake at Botmaskop and in the industry of gated estates in the Winelands. This project shows how rezoning agricultural land for a luxury gated estate has dramatically increased the value of the land. In 2003 the 31 hectares land was bought for just over 3 million Rands, ostensibly to develop a hotel for which it engaged in a prolonged public and state approval process. Twenty years later, the current developer, Staytus, buys the same piece of land for R200 million, now with zoning rights. It is bonded for R320 million. It was sold to Staytus by a company called Reset Properties who had bought it in 2017 for R14 million. Reset Properties falls under Foundation Capital which is an office owned by one of South Africa’s wealthiest families, and they were the ones who managed to get the non-substantive amendment passed in the provincial department of the Environmental Department. At the heart of this dispute are two conflicting visions over the future of Stellenbosch and the Winelands. One group – the wealthy property developers and their friends – want to create a safe space for the very rich, in the beautiful setting of the Winelands, through the ongoing building of gated estates, and the complimentary sponsorship of the town’s projects and aesthetic needs. The other would like to see Stellenbosch develop more slowly, where there is greater integration of the different economic groups, and the town develops sustainably on its own commercial success, respecting the beautiful spaces and agricultural land in which it is set. This is my interpretation after many discussions with people in the area and the town.
metadata.Further information: There are layers and layers of intrigues - here are some of them including unproven rumours 1) The Botmaskop Farm was auctioned very controversially in 2012 to a company called Lancelot Stellenbosch Mountain Retreat. The man behind the holding company was Cobus Kellermann who was accused by Alec Hogg of running the Belvedere Ponzi scheme. It turns out that it wasn’t a Ponzi scheme and Kellermann is sueing Alec Hogg for R5 million but has lost everything including Botmaskop in the process. It’s an extraordinary story – almost worth a Carte Blanche in its own right. But I don’t think it has bearing on this story if it is to be told in 10-12 minutes. 2) The developer, Werner Roux, has a very bad reputation as a person who bulldozes communities in order to get his developments through. He has been involved in a twenty year battle over the development of a site near George at the Maalgat River Mouth which he wanted to turn into two golf estates, and then into a sort of agricultural gentleman’s estate Utopia. A handful of locals have fought him tooth and nail all the way to the Constitutional Court and the matter is not yet resolved. However, it is suggested that he used his political connections to get approvals through the Agricultural Department and also petrol bomb a house of one of the opponents and loosen the screws of a BMW, as well as deliver a death threat in colloquial Afrikaans. Again, this does not have huge bearing on the story at hand. He has done and is busy with multiple projects in the Winelands. 3) There are plenty of rumours swirling around the Botmaskop development, which are juicy but not necessarily material because they can not be proven: a) That the development is in trouble financially and it has a silent, wealthy funder called Dennis Venter in Somerset West b) That a Russian or Russians have snapped up a few plots c) That the Municipal manager has got herself a plot behind the scenes
